title: ERP-WMS stock reconciliation note - July (cutoff timing only)
content: July ERP vs WMS stock gap of £980k was put down to cutoff timing only: WMS posts receipts 1-3 days after ERP records the inbound PO. No status-mapping or item-level analysis was done and no prevention step was agreed, so the gap came back. To be replaced by a fuller write-up and archived.

title: UK-Vietnam FTA: preferential origin rules for garments
content: UK-Vietnam FTA preferential duty on garments (HS 61/62) needs originating status under the product-specific rule: manufacture from yarn. The fabric itself must be knitted (chapter 61) or woven (chapter 62) in Vietnam or the UK (bilateral cumulation); cutting and sewing alone from imported fabric does not confer origin. A tolerance of up to 10% by weight of non-originating materials applies. Fabric from China is non-originating, so cut-and-sew in Vietnam from Chinese fabric does NOT qualify and pays full duty. To qualify: buy fabric knitted or woven in Vietnam or the UK, or knit/weave it in Vietnam from yarn; otherwise keep non-originating inputs under 10% by weight. Evidence: an origin declaration or a certificate of origin issued per shipment by the Vietnamese Ministry of Industry and Trade (or its authorised chamber), with commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading and fabric mill and yarn supplier declarations proving where the fabric was made. Customs holds the rules as ORG-910001 (knitted) and ORG-910002 (woven). Keep records 4 years.

title: Carrier tender scorecard: criteria, weights and disqualifying thresholds
content: Weight criteria by what has cost us most (damage and loss claims first, then delay and service failures), not by price alone. Recommended weights: on-time delivery 30%; damage and loss performance (claims rate and claim recovery) 25%; cost per shipment 20%; compliance and safety (insurance, operator licence) 10%; tracking and EDI visibility 10%; sustainability 5%. Score each criterion 1-5. Minimum thresholds that disqualify a bidder: on-time delivery below 90%; damage and loss rate above 1.0% of shipments; cargo liability cover below £100k per consignment; no live tracking or EDI feed; no current operator licence or safety accreditation. Review scores quarterly during the contract.

title: Returned goods and EPR rules: Germany, France, Netherlands
content: Germany (VerpackG, duty of care): register in LUCID and join a dual system before shipping packaging; usable returned goods must not be destroyed. Penalties up to £75k per breach plus sales ban. Reporting: annual data report to the Central Agency and quarterly volumes to the dual system. France (AGEC law): destroying unsold or returned non-food goods is banned, they must be reused, donated or recycled; EPR through Citeo (packaging) and Refashion (textiles); Triman recycling label required. Penalties up to £80k. Reporting: annual declaration of products placed on market and unsold-goods disposal. Netherlands: packaging EPR through Afvalfonds Verpakkingen; textile EPR scheme with producer registration; annual volume reporting. Penalties up to £65k. Strictest: France (destruction ban plus highest penalties). Likely conflicts for us: scrapping returned stock in France or Germany, and missing label or registration in each country.

title: Sourcing country disruption: warning signs, trigger points and contingencies
content: Watch list for our sourcing countries (China, Vietnam, India, Bangladesh, Turkey): export restrictions (India cotton or yarn export curbs), power shortages (rolling cuts or gas rationing in Bangladesh, northern Vietnam and southern China), political unrest (strikes, hartals or street protests near ports and industrial zones, mainly Bangladesh), typhoon season at Vietnamese ports, Turkey currency volatility. Recommended trigger points for action (any one): factory power cuts above 4 hours a day for 3 consecutive days; port or road blockade lasting over 48 hours; new export restriction covering our category; government travel advisory raised to essential travel only. Contingency when triggered: list open POs not yet shipped, bring shipments forward, air-freight the most urgent, move volume to alternate suppliers (Turkey, Portugal for short-lead items) and hold 2-3 weeks of buffer stock on best sellers. Review country risk quarterly.

title: Morocco vs Turkey nearshore sourcing comparison
content: Incentives: Morocco - EU association agreement (zero duty on originating goods), Tangier and Kenitra free zones with multi-year tax holidays, state training subsidies; Turkey - UK-Turkey FTA (zero duty on originating goods), regional investment incentives. Labour: Morocco has a smaller skilled garment workforce but wages 30-40% below Turkey; Turkey has a large skilled workforce but wages rising fast with inflation. Fabric: Morocco imports most fabric (Turkey, Spain, China), which can break origin rules; Turkey has integrated mills from yarn to fabric, best fabric availability. Risk: Morocco - stable politics, dirham managed against a EUR/USD basket so low currency risk; Turkey - lira volatile with high inflation, regional proximity to Syria and Iraq, earthquake exposure. Tailoring: Morocco is better for tailored suits and jackets (established tailoring lines for EU brands); Turkey is better for knitwear, denim and fast reorders. Lead time: Morocco 8-12 weeks and consistent; Turkey 6-10 weeks but variable. Cost premium vs Asia: Morocco 15-20%, Turkey 10-15%.

title: Co-development IP protection clauses
content: Recommended: Buyer owns all derivative IP; supplier retains pre-existing IP. Escrow for know-how transfer. Non-compete 2-year post-termination.

title: Supplier lead-time reduction programme: structure, retailer results, supplier needs
content: Structure (6-9 months): 1) baseline the order-to-ship lead time by step (fabric booking, cutting, sewing, QC, shipping booking), month 1; 2) quick wins live by month 3: remove approval waits, pre-position trims, release a rolling 12-week forecast; 3) process redesign months 3-6: line balancing, in-line QC, smaller batches, pilot on one line; 4) sustain: weekly lead-time KPI and quarterly review. Retailer results: peers cut lead time 15-25% (typically 18%); one cut 22% in 6 months for about £50k of consulting, saving about £200k a year (ROI 4:1). What the supplier needs from us: a rolling 12-week forecast accurate to +/-20%, a frozen firm-order window of 8 weeks, sample and approval turnaround under 5 days, early fabric and trim commitment, a shared KPI dashboard, a named buyer and QA owner, and joint workshops (sometimes shared training cost).

title: Supplier fraud schemes and red flags for onboarding
content: Schemes onboarding should catch: (1) bank-detail change or payment diversion - a genuine supplier's bank account is replaced, or a new supplier asks to be paid to a third-party or personal account; this is the most common scheme in retail and apparel sourcing; (2) fake certifications and audit reports - forged BSCI, ISO or product test certificates; (3) shell or front companies - no real factory, or a sanctioned owner hidden behind nominees; (4) conflict of interest and kickbacks - a buyer or approver linked to the supplier, with sudden large discounts below market used as bait; (5) duplicate or inflated invoices; (6) substitution of materials or undisclosed subcontracting. Controls: sanctions screening of company and beneficial owners; bank account verification by call-back to a known number with account-holder name match; certificate verification with the issuing body; conflict-of-interest declaration; trade finance verification; site audit before the first PO. Checks most often missing from onboarding: bank account name match and call-back, certificate verification with the issuer, and beneficial-ownership screening.

title: 3PL integration EDI API comparison
content: EDI: 4-6 weeks setup; £5k per year; 2-4 hour latency. API: 2-3 weeks setup; £15k initial plus £10k per year; real-time. File transfer: 1 week; less than £2k; manual risk. Risks: EDI - partner message mapping effort, dependence on a VAN, batch latency means stock and ASN data can be hours old. API - needs the 3PL to expose stable endpoints, rate limits and version changes, retry and monitoring to avoid lost or duplicate messages, highest run cost. File transfer - manual errors, no real-time view, file format drift and missing-file detection. Recommendation: API where the 3PL supports it and real-time stock matters; EDI for standard order and ASN flows; file transfer only as a short-term fallback.

title: Recycled nylon abrasion test failures
content: Trial recycled-nylon fabric failed abrasion tests at 50k cycles vs 100k target (Martindale); the first condition to fail was the high-load, 12 kPa abrasion step after the wash cycle. Root cause: lower fibre strength and shorter, more variable staple length in the recycled yarn, made worse by a loose, low-twist construction. Options: (1) blend 20 percent virgin nylon with recycled to maintain performance (material cost up 3 percent; performance meets spec); (2) raise yarn twist or use a higher denier yarn; (3) add a PU coating or DWR-compatible finish on the face. Re-test with a higher cycle count (at least 100k) after any change.

title: Technical finish performance gap lab to field
content: New durable water-repellent finish passes lab tests but fails in real-world wear trials: field performance drops after 5 washes. Lab conditions: controlled humidity, new fabric, standard spray-rating test with a single wash cycle; wear-trial conditions: real laundry with variable water hardness, detergent residue, tumble-drying heat, abrasion at elbows and shoulders, and sweat/body-oils contamination. Why: the finish is not durable to repeated laundering and surface abrasion, which the lab method does not reproduce. Solution: revise test to include actual fabric weight, agitation cycle, hard-water wash and tumble-dry between spray-rating checks, with abrasion pre-conditioning; predict field performance from the spray rating after 5 and 10 wash cycles.

title: Seam strength and water resistance jacket failures
content: First sample technical jacket misses seam strength spec (50N vs 65N required) and water resistance. Construction causes: (1) seam allowance too tight (increase by 3mm); (2) stitch density too high (over 5 stitches/cm) perforates the fabric and lets water through the needle holes; (3) seam tape not fully heat-sealed or too narrow (use 22mm tape, seal at the supplier's recommended temperature). Revisions to try: increase allowance by 3mm, reduce stitch density to 4 stitches/cm with a bonded seam tape, add a bar-tack at stress points. Re-run seam strength first (the allowance change drives both failures), then the water resistance (hydrostatic head) test on the revised construction.

title: Credit hold policy and customer payment terms
content: Credit hold policy: Customers more than 60 days overdue are placed on credit hold. Shipments paused until payment received or payment plan agreed. Legal review required before proceeding with recovery steps. Finance approval required for any hold release.

title: RFID and EAS tagging for shrink control
content: RFID tag and EAS (Electronic Article Surveillance) implementation reduces shrink by 30-40% when combined with layout optimization. Tagging cost: £0.15-£0.25 per unit. ROI: 2-3 months in high-shrink stores. Best practice: implement tags at receipt, use EAS gates at exit, combine with staff training.

title: Nearshore capacity commitments: how retailers structure priority-capacity deals
content: Typical structure: framework agreement with a committed minimum volume of about 60% of annual forecast (equal to 15-20% of the factory capacity, one dedicated line), the rest flexible; capacity reservation fee of 2-3% of committed value credited against orders; priority allocation in peak. Never commit above 70% of the low-case demand forecast or more than 30% of the supplier's capacity (dependency risk). Term 2-3 years. Clauses that protect us if demand drops: volume flexibility band of +/-20% on 8 weeks' notice, shortfall payment capped at 10% of committed value (take-or-pay), buy-back of finished goods and fabric bought against firm orders, rolling forecast that is non-binding beyond the frozen firm-order window, and termination for convenience on 90 days' notice.

title: Apparel supplier agreements: market norms and unusual terms
content: Normal in apparel: payment 30-60 days from goods receipt; liability capped at order value or 12 months of purchases, with product safety, death or injury, and IP claims uncapped; buyer owns designs and patterns, supplier keeps pre-existing know-how; force majeure excludes strikes, supplier financial failure and shipping delays; right to audit and a signed code of conduct; AQL inspection with right to reject. Unusual or red flags: payment terms over 90 days or payment before shipment; liability capped below order value or excluding product safety; supplier keeping IP in our designs or free to resell them; subcontracting without consent (main social-compliance risk); price changes after order confirmation; minimum volume commitments or exclusivity binding us; no audit right; auto-renewal beyond 12 months.

title: AMR fleet firmware update, rollback and safety re-validation runbook
content: Update: pilot on 2 robots for 48 hours, then roll out zone by zone with the fleet manager (about 30 minutes per zone). Keep the previous firmware image (4.6) on the fleet manager for 30 days. Rollback: stop dispatch to the zone, select the previous image and push it to the robots (about 15 minutes per robot, batches of 5); trigger it if more than 2 robot faults a day or localisation errors appear. Safety: any firmware change touching navigation or safety-rated lidar zones requires the HSE safety validation to be re-run (emergency stop, speed and separation monitoring, zone stop) before robots return to service; allow 2 days per zone. Peak: change freeze starts mid-November, so firmware changes must land by the first week of November, and not during peak trading weeks.

title: Force majeure and port closures: how courts have treated claims
content: Internal legal note summarising counsel advice on disputes since 2020 (pandemic port shutdowns, the Suez Canal blockage, Red Sea diversions). Courts apply force majeure clauses strictly by their wording. Where a clause names port closures, as our standard Force Majeure clause (CLS-001) does, a closure that actually prevents performance usually qualifies. Courts have rejected claims where: (1) the closure only made performance slower or more expensive, for example rerouting to another port or around the Cape, higher freight or demurrage - cost and delay alone are not force majeure; (2) the claimant could not show mitigation such as an alternative port or air freight; (3) notice was late - missing the contractual notice window has defeated otherwise valid claims; (4) the cause was congestion or a strike, which is not a closure unless the clause says so. Implications for our clause: it covers port closures and already excludes strikes and shipping delays, keeps 48-hour notice and a 90-day termination right. Recommended changes: define a port closure as an official closure or blockade by the port authority or government lasting more than 72 hours; state that rerouting, higher cost or delay alone are not force majeure; require the claiming party to evidence mitigation within 7 days.

title: Supplier liability caps for product-safety claims: market practice and counter-position
content: Market practice: retailers accept a supplier cap at the value of the order, or at 12 months of purchases, for ordinary commercial claims such as late delivery or price disputes. Product-safety claims (death, personal injury, recall costs and third-party claims) are normally uncapped, because consumer-protection law makes the retailer liable to the customer whatever the contract says, so a capped supplier leaves us carrying the excess. A cap at order value is therefore not reasonable for product safety: recall, testing and injury costs can far exceed the value of one order. Recommended counter: (1) product safety, death or personal injury, recall costs and IP infringement uncapped; (2) general cap at the higher of 100% of the order value and 12 months of purchases; (3) supplier holds Product Liability insurance of at least GBP 5m for apparel and food (GBP 1m other) with Harbour & Vale named as additional insured; (4) supplier indemnifies recall costs. Never accept a cap below the supplier's insurance cover.

title: Shrink controls: security guarding, CCTV and POS system rules
content: Evidence from the same 50-store, 12-month study as the cost-benefit analysis. Security guard (one guard at peak hours): cost £45k per year per store. Shrink: 0.8% to 0.7% (annual saving £30k). Payback: about 18 months; deters visible theft but does little against internal loss. CCTV upgrade: cost £12k one-time. Shrink: 0.8% to 0.72% (saving £24k). Payback: 6 months. System rules (POS exception reporting: refund, void and discount thresholds, manager override and stock-adjustment controls): cost £6k setup + £1k per year. Shrink: 0.8% to 0.65% (saving £45k). Payback: under 2 months; best against internal and till-related loss. Ranking by shrink saved per pound spent: system rules, tagging, layout, CCTV, staffing, security guards.

title: Third-party and supplier connections: risk ranking and quick controls
content: Rank supplier and partner connections by access first, then exposure: (1) direct or privileged access to ERP, WMS or vendor master and bank detail screens; (2) connections that carry orders, ASNs or payment data (EDI, API, SFTP); (3) read-only portals. Highest risk is a shared or privileged account with no MFA and no IP restriction. Quickest controls, in order: enforce MFA on every portal and partner account (days); restrict access by IP allowlist or VPN (days); remove standing privileged access and use least-privilege roles with time-limited approval (1-2 weeks); alert on logins from new locations and on vendor bank detail changes (1-2 weeks); rotate API keys and SFTP credentials every 90 days and remove unused accounts (2-4 weeks). Bank detail changes must always be verified by call-back to a known phone number. Review high-risk connections quarterly.
